analogy.p: Think of the sea as a sculptor with a hammer and chisel (erosion) and also a delivery driver (deposition). The sculptor chips hardest at the weakest, most exposed parts of a block of stone, forming headlands, caves, arches and stacks. The driver drops off sand and pebbles wherever the lorry slows down, building beaches, spits and bars. This works because the same source (wave energy) both removes and delivers material. It breaks down because the sea has no plan or intention: its work depends only on rock resistance and wave energy.
analogy.t: A sculptor and a delivery driver

bullets: **Erosional landforms** are made when waves wear rock away: headlands and bays, cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks and stumps.
**Depositional landforms** are made when waves lose energy and drop sediment: beaches, sand dunes, spits and bars.
**Rock type** (geology) controls where erosion is fast and slow; **wave energy** controls whether the sea erodes or deposits.
Exam answers need a logical **sequence** (first, then, eventually) and named **processes**, not just a description of the finished shape.
Sketch maps and annotated diagrams are an expected skill and earn marks when each label is linked to a process.
Landforms of erosion are mostly found on **high-energy coasts** with strong, destructive waves and long fetch.
Landforms of deposition are found on **low-energy** stretches, in sheltered bays or where the coast changes direction.
**Link to other topics:** the processes (hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, solution, longshore drift) are in the previous point, and the management of these landforms follows in the next.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA expects you to describe the **characteristics** and explain the **formation** of landforms made by erosion (**headlands and bays, cliffs and wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks**) and by deposition (**beaches, sand dunes, spits and bars**). You must also be able to use **an example of a section of UK coastline** to identify its major landforms of erosion and deposition. Every landform is explained by the same small set of ideas: the type of rock, the energy of the waves, the process acting (erosion, transport or deposition) and time. If you understand these, you can build an explanation for any landform rather than memorising separate stories.

bullets: **Hydraulic action** needs cracks in the rock and is strongest in high-energy, breaking waves.
**Abrasion** needs loose sediment as 'tools'; it is usually the main process cutting wave-cut notches and platforms.
**Attrition** does not erode the cliff; it reduces the size of load and makes beach material smaller and rounder.
**Solution** is chemical, so it matters most on chalk and limestone; it is not affected by wave energy as much as the others.
**Weathering** is breakdown in place; **erosion** involves removal by a moving agent. Do not confuse them.
**Transport** includes traction, saltation, suspension and solution; **longshore drift** moves material along the coast in a zigzag.
**Deposition** happens when waves lose energy (shallow water, sheltered bays, change of coastline direction, low wind) or when supply of sediment is large.
**Constructive waves** (low, long, swash stronger than backwash) build beaches; **destructive waves** (tall, steep, backwash stronger than swash) remove them.
core.h: The processes you need to apply
core.p: Landforms are the result of processes, so the key vocabulary must be used precisely. **Erosion** is the wearing away of the land by the sea. **Hydraulic action** is the force of water crashing into cracks, compressing air inside them, so that the pressure weakens the rock and pieces break off. **Abrasion** is the sea hurling rock fragments (sand, pebbles, boulders) against the cliff, scraping and wearing it away like sandpaper. **Attrition** is rocks knocking against each other and becoming smaller and rounder. **Solution** is the dissolving of soluble rocks, such as chalk and limestone, by slightly acidic sea water. **Weathering** (such as freeze-thaw and biological weathering) weakens the cliff from above and from within, and **mass movement** (rock falls, slumping, landslides) brings the weakened material down.

bullets: Resistant rock: slow erosion, steep cliffs, headlands, stacks. Less resistant rock: fast erosion, bays, gentler slopes.
**Concordant coast:** rock bands parallel to the coast; hard rock forms a barrier, then once breached the soft rock behind erodes into a cove. Example: Lulworth Cove, Dorset.
**Discordant coast:** rock bands perpendicular to the coast; produces alternating headlands and bays. Example: Swanage Bay and the chalk headlands, Dorset.
**Joints, faults and bedding planes** are weaknesses where hydraulic action and weathering concentrate and caves form.
Rock type also affects cliff shape: clay cliffs slump and have a rounded profile; chalk cliffs are steep and white with a clean face.
The same wave energy produces different results on different rocks, so always name the rock when you explain.
The speed of erosion is not constant. Storms deliver a large part of the total retreat in a short time.
**Higher-level thinking:** a stretch of coast is a balance between the resistance of the rock and the energy of the waves; if either changes, the landforms change.
core.h: Geology and the shape of the coast
core.p: The coastline is not eroded evenly because rocks differ in **resistance**. Hard, resistant rocks such as granite, chalk and limestone, wear away slowly and form steep cliffs and headlands. Soft, less resistant rocks such as clay and sand are eroded quickly and form bays, gentle slopes and often slumping cliffs. The pattern of the rock relative to the coast also matters. On a **concordant coastline** bands of hard and soft rock run parallel to the sea, so the hard rock protects the soft rock behind it until the sea breaches it. On a **discordant coastline** bands of rock lie at right angles to the coast, so differential erosion makes headlands and bays directly. The structure of the rock, including joints, bedding planes and faults, creates lines of weakness which waves exploit first.

bullets: **Headland:** a high, steep piece of land made of resistant rock that juts out into the sea.
**Bay:** a curved, sheltered indentation in the coast, usually with a beach, formed in less resistant rock.
**Step 1:** hard and soft rock outcrop along the coast and meet the sea.
**Step 2:** the soft rock is eroded faster (hydraulic action, abrasion), forming a bay; the hard rock is left sticking out as a headland.
**Step 3:** waves refract into the bay and focus energy on the headland sides, so the headland is attacked by erosion.
**Step 4:** in the bay the waves lose energy so sand is deposited and forms a beach, which protects the bay from further erosion.
Over time the headland is eroded to form caves, arches and stacks, so these landforms are linked.
**Example:** Swanage Bay (soft clay and sand) lies between chalk headlands at Ballard Down and the Foreland in Dorset.
core.p: Where a coast has alternating bands of hard and soft rock, differential erosion forms **headlands and bays**. The soft rock (clay, sand) is eroded faster by hydraulic action and abrasion and is cut back to form a **bay**. The resistant rock (chalk, limestone) is eroded more slowly and sticks out into the sea as a **headland**. As the headlands stick out, waves **refract** (bend) around them, so wave energy is concentrated on the headlands, increasing erosion there, while energy is spread out in the bay. The lower energy in the bay means deposition, so the bay often has a sandy beach that protects the soft rock behind from further erosion.

bullets: **Step 1:** weathering weakens the cliff; waves attack the base, focusing erosion between high and low tide.
**Step 2:** hydraulic action and abrasion cut a **wave-cut notch** in the cliff foot.
**Step 3:** as the notch deepens the cliff above becomes unstable and **collapses** by rock fall or slumping.
**Step 4:** the collapsed rock is broken down by attrition and carried away by the sea or deposited as beach material.
**Step 5:** repeated notch cutting and collapse make the cliff retreat; the exposed base is the **wave-cut platform**.
The platform is **gently sloping (about 1 to 3 degrees)** and may be several metres to hundreds of metres wide; the wider it is, the less wave energy reaches the cliff, which can slow retreat.
Cliff profile depends on rock type and structure: rock that dips towards the sea tends to slide; horizontal layers give vertical cliffs.
**Link:** a wave-cut platform plus a stretch of failed cliff may be exposed at low tide as 'ledges', and can be crossed on foot at low tide.
core.p: A **cliff** is a steep rock face at the coast. Cliffs form when waves attack the base of the land. Most of the energy of breaking waves is delivered at the foot of the cliff, where **hydraulic action** and **abrasion** cut a **wave-cut notch** between the high and low tide marks. The rock above the notch is left unsupported, develops cracks and eventually collapses under gravity (a rock fall). The cliff therefore **retreats** inland. The flat or gently sloping area of rock left at the foot of the retreating cliff is the **wave-cut platform**. It is exposed at low tide and often covered with rock pools, boulders and a thin layer of beach material, which is also used as ammunition for abrasion. Fallen material is broken down by attrition and carried away.

bullets: **Crack / line of weakness** (joint or fault) in the headland is attacked by hydraulic action.
**Cave:** hydraulic action and abrasion widen the crack; it deepens as waves hurl material at the back.
**Arch:** the cave is eroded right through the headland or two caves meet from either side.
**Stack:** the arch roof is weakened by weathering and erosion and collapses, leaving a tall column of rock separated from the headland.
**Stump:** the stack's base is undercut and the stack collapses leaving a low rock outcrop, visible only at low tide.
Each stage is faster in softer or heavily jointed rock; resistant rock like limestone makes arches that can last a long time.
The sequence needs a **headland**, so link it with headlands and bays: they are not separate topics.
**Examples:** Durdle Door (arch, Dorset), Old Harry Rocks (stacks and stumps, Dorset).
core.p: This is a classic sequence that happens on **headlands** because they are exposed to concentrated wave energy. **Hydraulic action** and **abrasion** attack a weakness such as a crack or fault in the headland, widening it into a **cave**. Over time the sea keeps eroding the back of the cave while weathering attacks its roof, until the cave is cut right through the headland, forming an **arch**. The arch roof is weakened by weathering (for example freeze-thaw) and by erosion at its base, until it can no longer support its own weight and the roof **collapses**. The part of the headland left standing is a **stack**, a tall column of rock separated from the land. The stack is attacked at its base by waves, undercut and eventually collapses to leave a low, flat **stump** which may only be visible at low tide.

bullets: **Sandy beaches:** found in sheltered bays; sand particles are small so water is retained and backwash drags material back, giving a gentle gradient.
**Shingle beaches:** large stones, steeper; water drains quickly through the pebbles, so the backwash is weak and swash deposits.
**Berm:** a ridge at the top of the beach marking the highest reach of normal waves; storm berm is higher.
**Ridges and runnels** (low ridges and shallow channels) can form on the foreshore of a sandy beach.
Material tends to be **sorted**: larger pebbles at the top of the beach, finer sand lower down (where the waves are weaker).
Beaches are **dynamic**: they change daily with tides and with storms, and seasonally (summer constructive, winter destructive).
A beach protects the cliff behind by absorbing wave energy, so beaches are valuable for **coastal defence** and for tourism.
**Link:** beach nourishment and groynes in management rely on the idea that beaches are a natural defence.
core.p: A **beach** is a deposit of sediment (sand, shingle or pebbles) between the lowest tide and the highest storm waves. Beaches form where waves lose energy and deposit material, usually in sheltered bays or where supply of sediment is large. The sediment is eroded from cliffs or brought by longshore drift and rivers. **Constructive waves** have a strong swash and weak backwash, so they push material up the beach and build it up. **Destructive waves** have a strong backwash and weak swash, so they drag material down and flatten the beach. Beach shape reflects sediment size: sandy beaches are wide and gentle, shingle beaches are narrow and steep.

bullets: **Conditions:** a wide, gently sloping sandy beach, a large supply of sand, onshore wind, and an obstacle to trap sand.
**Embryo dunes:** the first small mounds of sand trapped by an obstacle and pioneer plants, near the high-tide line.
**Fore (yellow) dunes:** higher, colonised by marram grass; the roots bind the sand, and the dune grows upward.
**Grey (fixed) dunes:** further inland, more stable; humus from dead plants makes the soil richer, so more species grow.
This is **plant succession**: each stage changes the conditions for the next (more shelter, more humus, less salt).
Gaps in the dunes (**blowouts**) can be caused by trampling by walkers or storms and let the wind erode the sand.
Dunes are a natural **defence** against the sea and habitat for rare species, so they are often protected by fencing and planting marram.
**Example:** Studland Bay, Dorset, has an extensive dune system.
core.p: **Sand dunes** are hills of wind-blown sand found at the back of wide sandy beaches. They need a large supply of sand, strong onshore winds and a wide beach that dries out at low tide so the wind can move it. Sand is blown up the beach until it meets an obstacle such as driftwood or seaweed, then it is deposited in the shelter of the obstacle. Pioneer plants, for example sand couch grass, colonise the sand, and their roots and stems trap more sand, forming **embryo dunes**. As the dunes grow they are colonised by **marram grass**, which is tolerant of salt, drought and burial and grows upwards through the sand. This stabilises the dune as **fore dunes** or **yellow dunes**. Further back, plants add humus, so older dunes become fixed (**grey dunes**) and support more plants.

bullets: **Step 1:** longshore drift moves sediment along the coast (waves approach at an angle with the prevailing wind).
**Step 2:** at a change in coastline direction (headland end, bay, estuary) the sediment is carried out into deeper water beyond the coast.
**Step 3:** the water is deeper and the waves lose energy, so sediment is **deposited** and builds up as a ridge above sea level, extending the spit.
**Step 4:** a secondary wind or wave direction curves the end, making a **recurved end**.
**Step 5:** behind the spit the water is sheltered; silt and mud settle and **salt marsh** develops.
A spit grows only while there is a steady supply of sediment and is destroyed by storms or if the supply is cut off.
**Examples:** Spurn Head (Holderness coast, mouth of the Humber estuary), Hurst Castle spit (Hampshire).
**Link:** salt marshes are valuable wildlife habitats and also absorb wave energy.
core.p: A **spit** is a long, narrow finger of sand or shingle that is attached to the land at one end and extends out into the sea or across the mouth of an estuary at the other. Spits form where the coastline changes direction sharply (for example at a bend, at a river mouth or at a bay) and where **longshore drift** is active. Waves move sediment along the coast in a zigzag. When the coast turns away, the sediment continues in the original direction and is deposited in the sheltered water where the waves lose energy. The deposited material builds up into a ridge above sea level. A change in wind or wave direction can curve the end, forming a **recurved end** (hook). In the sheltered water behind the spit, the water is calm and fine sediment collects to form mudflats and **salt marsh**.

bullets: **Bar:** a depositional ridge of sand or shingle across a bay, linking two headlands.
**Lagoon:** a body of water cut off from the sea behind a bar. It slowly silts up.
A bar is essentially a **spit that has grown right across** a bay; a **tombolo** is a bar linking the mainland to an island.
Formation: longshore drift → spit grows across a bay → joins the opposite headland → lagoon forms behind.
Bars are dynamic and can be breached by storms and rising sea level; the shingle may roll back (rollover) in storms.
**Examples:** Slapton Sands (Devon) has a bar enclosing Slapton Ley; Chesil Beach (Dorset) is a shingle barrier beach about 29 km long.
Because the lagoon is fresh or brackish, it supports specialised wildlife, so bars often have conservation designations.
Bars cause problems for management: the bar and the road or settlements on it are at risk from erosion and flooding.
core.p: A **bar** is a ridge of sand or shingle that has grown across a bay, joining two headlands, so that it seals off the bay from the open sea. A bar forms when a **spit** keeps growing across a bay until it connects the two sides. The body of water trapped behind is called a **lagoon**, and it gradually fills with sediment and plants, forming marsh. Bars are formed by the same process as spits: longshore drift supplies sediment, and deposition occurs where the energy is low. Bars may also be built by waves pushing sediment onshore as sea level rises after the last ice age.

bullets: Name your chosen example, then list **erosional landforms** (headlands, cliffs, platforms, caves, arches, stacks) and **depositional landforms** (beaches, dunes, spits, bars) found there.
State the **geology** behind each landform (for example hard chalk and Portland limestone, soft clay and sand).
Use place names: Lulworth Cove, Durdle Door, Old Harry Rocks, Swanage Bay, Studland Bay, Chesil Beach.
Use **OS map** evidence: tightly spaced contour lines show cliffs; a blue dotted low-water line shows platforms; a hooked line shows a spit.
Relate each landform to the **processes** that formed it and the **rock type**.
Explain the link between landforms: bays and headlands, then caves, arches and stacks, then stumps.
A good case study answer includes **named places, a process and a reason**.
If you studied a different example (for example Holderness or the Norfolk coast), use the same structure with your own named landforms.
core.h: A UK example: the Dorset coast
core.p: The Dorset (Jurassic) coast is widely used as an example of a section of UK coastline because it shows many landforms in a short distance. Hard and soft rock outcrop in bands, so the coast shows concordant and discordant sections. At **Lulworth Cove**, waves breached the resistant Portland limestone and eroded the softer clays and sands behind to form a near-circular cove. **Durdle Door** is an arch in Portland limestone. At **Old Harry Rocks**, near Swanage, chalk headlands have been cut into stacks and stumps. **Swanage Bay**, of soft clay and sand, lies between chalk headlands, and **Studland Bay** has a wide sandy beach with a dune system behind it. **Chesil Beach** is a long shingle bar. Whichever example you use, be ready to annotate a sketch map with landforms and explain each one.

bullets: **Describe** means say what it looks like (shape, height, features); **explain** means say how and why, using processes.
Use **annotated diagrams** to earn marks: label hydraulic action, abrasion, notch and so on, and add a caption.
In a '**how** has a landform formed' answer, always include a **sequence** and a **process word** in each step.
Use **key terms**: resistant, less resistant, differential erosion, wave refraction, longshore drift, deposition, swash, backwash.
On OS maps, quote **grid references** (four or six figures) when asked to locate a landform.
A **sketch map** should be neat, show a title, north arrow if needed, and labels linked with lines.
Use named examples with place names to reach top levels in 6-mark questions.
Practise drawing the cave-arch-stack sequence and the spit diagram from memory.
core.h: Exam skills: sketches, maps and data
core.p: Questions on coastal landforms use a mixture of photos, diagrams, OS maps and sketches. You are expected to **identify** a landform from a photograph (for example a stack or arch), **describe** its characteristics (shape, size, rock) and **explain** how it formed. For 4 mark questions, write a clear sequence of steps with processes. For a 6 mark question you also need a conclusion or an assessment. On an OS map, recognise coastal landforms from contour patterns, symbols and shapes: cliffs are shown with black hachures or very close contours, rock platforms and sand and shingle are labelled, spits are long narrow features extending from the land, and dunes are marked as sand with a dotted pattern.

bullets: Landforms respond to changes in **sea level, storms, sediment supply** and human actions.
Cliff retreat rates vary: soft clay may retreat by metres a year, hard rock by millimetres.
Defences change sediment movement, so a groyne on one beach may starve a beach down the coast of sand.
Dunes and salt marshes can be managed as natural defences by fencing, planting and leaving them alone.
**Climate change** raises sea level and increases storminess, which increases erosion and flooding risk.
The balance of erosion and deposition determines whether the coast is advancing or retreating.
Link to **geo.2.3**: the next point covers hard and soft engineering and a coastal management case study.
In extended answers, show that you understand **cause and effect** between processes, landforms and human impacts.
core.h: Linking landforms to management and change
core.p: Coastal landforms are not fixed: they are constantly changing because of natural processes, sea-level rise and human actions. Cliffs retreat, spits grow or breach, dunes migrate and beaches rise and fall. This matters because people live and work on the coast. Where soft cliffs are retreating, homes and roads are at risk, so people try to protect them with hard or soft engineering. Defences, though, can interrupt the supply of sediment (for example groynes trap sand on one side) and cause increased erosion elsewhere. Understanding how a landform forms helps you understand how it responds to management, which is the focus of the next spec point.

exam: **Describe** (1 to 2 marks): say what it looks like, give shape, size and rock type. Do not explain.

**Explain how a landform formed** (4 marks): write 4 linked steps (for example crack, cave, arch, stack) naming hydraulic action, abrasion and weathering; each correct step with a process scores a mark.
**6-mark extended answers:** state the order, name processes, mention rock type and wave energy, use a named example, and finish with a short conclusion.
Use connectives such as **first, then, as a result, eventually** to show the sequence.
A labelled sketch can score marks if each label is linked to a process; add a short caption.
On a photograph, identify the landform, then give two features that prove it (for example 'tall, isolated column').
**OS map questions:** give six-figure grid references; contour lines close together = steep cliff; use the scale to measure the width of a platform or spit.
**Sketch map:** include a title, north arrow if needed, and labels with arrows.
**Compare** a spit and a bar (4 marks): both formed by longshore drift and deposition; a bar crosses a bay and encloses a lagoon, a spit does not.
Use **specific named examples** (Durdle Door, Old Harry Rocks, Studland Bay) in extended answers to move into the top level.
Always give **reasons**, using 'because', 'so', 'therefore'. Do not just list.
Manage time: about one minute per mark.

mistakes.r: Hydraulic action is the force of water compressing air in cracks, which weakens the rock and breaks pieces off.
mistakes.w: Hydraulic action is the sea washing the rock away.

mistakes.r: It is an erosional landform left when a cliff retreats after the notch is cut and collapses.
mistakes.w: The wave-cut platform is formed by deposition.

mistakes.r: The arch roof is weakened by weathering and erosion at its base, then collapses under gravity, leaving a stack.
mistakes.w: Stacks form when arches are eroded away by the wind.

mistakes.r: Caves form by repeated hydraulic action and abrasion exploiting a weakness, over a long time.
mistakes.w: Caves are made by one big wave.

mistakes.r: Headlands are made of resistant (hard) rock that erodes more slowly; bays form in soft rock.
mistakes.w: Headlands are made of soft rock.

mistakes.r: Spits form by deposition where waves lose energy at a change in coastline direction, supplied by longshore drift.
mistakes.w: A spit forms when erosion is high.

mistakes.r: Mark schemes want a sequence: crack, cave, arch, stack, stump, with processes in each stage.
mistakes.w: Describing the end result only (a stack is a column of rock).

mistakes.r: Longshore drift is the net movement of material along the coast produced by swash at an angle and backwash straight down.
mistakes.w: Longshore drift is the same as the backwash.

mistakes.r: Dunes are formed by wind blowing dry sand up the beach, trapped by obstacles and plants.
mistakes.w: Sand dunes are formed by the sea.

summary: You must describe and explain how coastal landforms of erosion (headlands and bays, cliffs and wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks) and of deposition (beaches, sand dunes, spits, bars) form, and use a UK example to identify them. It matters because these are repeated 4 and 6 mark questions and underpin coastal management.

terms.d: A high, steep piece of land made of resistant rock that juts out into the sea.
A curved, sheltered indentation of the coast, usually made in less resistant rock, often with a beach.
Different rates of erosion of different rock types, with soft rock eroded faster than hard rock.
The bending of waves as they approach a coast, concentrating energy on headlands and spreading it in bays.
A groove cut at the base of a cliff between high and low tide by hydraulic action and abrasion.
A gently sloping area of rock left at the foot of a retreating cliff, exposed at low tide.
A hollow in a cliff or headland made by waves exploiting a weakness such as a crack.
A natural bridge of rock left when a cave is eroded right through a headland.
A tall column of rock left standing in the sea when the roof of an arch collapses.
A low remnant of a stack, often visible only at low tide.
The zigzag movement of material along the coast by swash (at the angle of the wave) and backwash (straight down the beach).
A long narrow ridge of sand or shingle attached to the land at one end and extending into the sea or across an estuary.
A ridge of sand or shingle that has grown across a bay, joining two headlands and enclosing a lagoon.
A body of water cut off from the sea by a bar.
A low wave with a long wavelength and strong swash that builds up a beach.
A tall, steep wave with a strong backwash that erodes a beach.
A mound of wind-blown sand, stabilised by vegetation such as marram grass.
A coastal wetland of mud and salt-tolerant plants that develops in sheltered water behind a spit.

worked.ans: Waves attack the cliff foot using hydraulic action and abrasion, cutting a wave-cut notch between the high and low tide marks (1). The rock above the notch is unsupported, so it becomes unstable and collapses under gravity (1). The cliff therefore retreats inland (1). The gently sloping area of rock left at the foot of the cliff is the wave-cut platform, and the collapsed material is broken down by attrition and removed (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain how a wave-cut platform is formed. (4 marks)
steps: Waves attack the base of the cliff between high and low tide.
Hydraulic action and abrasion cut a notch.
The rock above is unsupported and collapses; the cliff retreats.
The base left behind is a gently sloping platform.

worked.ans: Hydraulic action and abrasion widen a crack or weakness in the headland into a cave (1). The cave deepens until it breaks through the headland, forming an arch (1). Weathering and erosion at the base weaken the arch roof (1), which collapses, leaving a stack (a tall column of rock) separated from the headland (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain how a stack is formed from a headland. (4 marks)
steps: Crack in the headland attacked by hydraulic action.
Widened to a cave by abrasion.
Cave erodes through to give an arch.

worked.ans: Waves approach the coast at an angle, so swash and backwash move sediment along the coast by longshore drift (1). Where the coastline changes direction, for example at an estuary, the sediment continues straight on (1). In the deeper, sheltered water the waves lose energy so sediment is deposited and builds up into a ridge above sea level (1). A change in wind or wave direction can form a recurved end, and salt marsh forms in the sheltered water behind (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain how a spit is formed. (4 marks)
steps: Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast.
